lesson:
Introduction to Neural Networks

Machine learning is a broad category where a machine takes data and develops a model to make predictions. This contrasts with traditional rule-based programming, where humans describe all computer behaviors using rules and data. In machine learning, the approach is based on data and answers (training labels), and the machine develops its own formulas and algorithms to generate rules or a model. Machine learning algorithms come in different flavors, including regression (calculating a numerical value using statistical data), classification (categorizing categorical data), and clustering (where the computer infers information without supervised data).

Neural networks are motivated by the limitations of traditional algorithms like linear regression. While linear regression is great for tuning parameters based on data, it is limited by the structure of the data. For complex data like images—where a computer sees only a vast number of numeric values and where processing shapes is non-linear—linear regression is insufficient. Artificial neural networks (ANNs) were inspired by modeling how the human brain works. This was influenced by the one algorithm hypothesis, which suggests that much of the brain's incredible complexity may be explained by one underlying technique or principle. Evidence for this flexibility includes animal studies where the auditory cortex or somatosensory cortex, when severed and connected to visual sensors, learned how to process sight.

The building block of a neural network is an artificial neuron, simulated using a perceptron. A biological neuron consists of dendrites (inputs), a nucleus (cell body), and an axon (output) with axon terminals that connect to other neurons. Similarly, a perceptron uses inputs (x) as the equivalent of dendrites, weights (w) to determine the importance of information, a cell body to sum up weights and a bias, and an output axon that can signal downstream neurons. 

Neural networks organize these perceptrons into vertical blocks called layers. The first layer is the input layer, followed by one or more hidden layers (so-called because they are not directly visible from the input or output), and finally an output layer. In a densely connected neural network, each neuron in a layer is connected to every neuron in the downstream layer.

Training a neural network involves discovering the correct weighting values for each perceptron through trial and error. The model makes a prediction using training data, and a loss score is calculated to determine how far off the prediction was. This loss feeds back into the neural network to update the weights on the inputs. Once trained, the model has established weights and can process similar new data efficiently. A major advantage of neural networks is their performance growth curve: while other machine learning algorithms plateau as data size increases, neural networks continue to get better and more accurate as they receive more data.

Despite their advantages, neural networks have downsides. They are hard to explain (lack explainability), require massive amounts of data to be effective, and are expensive and time-consuming to train, requiring intense computer resources.

A classic machine learning challenge for neural networks is the MNIST data set, a collection of handwritten numbers from 0 through 9. To solve this, the data set is split into training and testing sets. During training, images are paired with their correct labels using a technique called one-hot encoding, where specific output perceptrons correspond to desired values (such as expecting the output node for zero to activate when a zero is inputted). The network adjusts its weights during training to better recognize patterns. Once trained, testing data without labels is passed through to evaluate how accurately the model identifies the numbers. Interactive tools and models built for the MNIST data set demonstrate this character recognition, often utilizing pre-processing steps to align edges and improve detection accuracy.

questions.question: Which type of programming relies on humans describing all of the behaviors of the computer using rules and data?
Which machine learning algorithm flavor is focused on calculating a numerical value using statistical data?
What is the name of the theory suggesting that much of the brain's complexity may be explained by one underlying technique?
What computational device is used as a simulator for a neuron in an artificial neural network?
What is the name of the layer in a neural network that is situated between the input and output layers and is not directly visible from either?
What is a major performance advantage of neural networks compared to other machine learning algorithms?
options: Neural networks require significantly less data than any other algorithm.
Neural networks continue to improve as more data is provided, whereas other algorithms plateau.
Neural networks are always cheaper and faster to train than linear regression.
Neural networks are completely immune to the explainability problem.
questions.correctAnswer: Neural networks continue to improve as more data is provided, whereas other algorithms plateau.
